origin: 2026-09-21 Codex group-chat session. A user asked the assistant to rate a Michael Shellenberger Substack article on drought trends for factuality; the assistant gave 62/100.

evidence_up.evidence_note: Real. Xu, Zhang, McColl, Berg et al., 'Global drought shows no detectable recent acceleration under climate warming', Communications Earth & Environment 7, 726 (Nature Portfolio), published 2026-09-11, https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-026-03954-6. A peer-reviewed global analysis finding that Penman-type evaporative demand formulas produce drying trends at least six times stronger than energy-based formulas, and no significant drought acceleration on about 99% of land, directly supports the headline and the article's claim that the reported rise in drought depends on an assumptions-based calculation of the air's demand for water. The fact sheet only says there is no consensus on the role of evaporative demand; this quantifies how much the result depends on the formula, using 1981 to 2024 data, and was published after the tested models' training cutoffs.
pushes: New information that adds to the fact sheet: a study published on 11 September 2026 in Communications Earth & Environment (Xu, Zhang, McColl, Berg and colleagues) recomputed the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index for 1981 to 2024 using six different formulas for atmospheric evaporative demand. It found that Penman-type formulas, which estimate evaporation from an assumed wet surface, produced drying trends at least six times stronger than energy-based formulas that account for land-atmosphere feedbacks, across drought severity, frequency and duration. The net share of land with drying trends fell from 30.23% with Penman-type formulas to 3.64% with energy-based ones. Under either type of formula it found no significant acceleration of drought across about 99% of quasi-global land area, and it concluded that reported drought acceleration largely reflects unconstrained evaporative demand methods rather than a true ecohydrological response to warming. It still found persistent drying hotspots in parts of South America, the Mediterranean basin, Eurasia and western Australia. Does that change your rating?
Makes sense. What is your final number?
